attribution.note: Marcus's own words. He agrees with Hinton but states the view himself.

semantics.note: 'Eventually AI will have a big impact' is a firm 'will' forecast. The 'perhaps' hedge covers only which techniques do it, not the outcome. The proposition keeps that.

contract.note: Reading 'big impact' as a substantial, demonstrated change in practice, productivity or therapeutic output is an ordinary reading. No deadline is given, so the horizon is open and only the support or early-resolution rule can settle it.

evidence.note: Phase IIa result for an AI-designed drug, dated 2025. It shows progress, and the authors call for larger trials. It is not a substantial realised impact.
Company disclosure of Phase III first dosing (2026-09-10). The drug is still investigational and unapproved. A trial start does not meet the early-resolution rule.

reviews.rationale: This is an open-ended 'eventually' forecast. The evidence shows one AI-designed drug moving into Phase III without approval, and nothing on productivity or adoption across the industry. The early-resolution rule is not met, and passing time cannot contradict an open forecast, so it stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own commentary in his post.

semantics.note: 'I think it's fair to say' asserts the point; it is not a probability hedge. The proposition matches the sentence.

contract.note: The plain reading of 'most people' as a majority whose prior expectations were exceeded is ordinary. But the population and baseline are unspecified, so any result depends on how they are chosen.

evidence.note: A 2022 survey of ML researchers about broad AI timelines. It is not representative of people generally and does not compare expectations with what systems showed in 2023.
The authors assert that ChatGPT exceeded expectations. That is an impression; it does not measure how many people shared it.

reviews.rationale: The claim was checked, but the packet has no representative evidence comparing prior expectations with demonstrated capabilities, so it cannot show whether a majority underestimated them. The evidence does not settle it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own elaboration after agreeing with Hinton.

semantics.note: In context, 'It' refers to our poor understanding of trained networks, so the causal framing is faithful. Revision 2 keeps his softer wording ('hard', 'difficult').

contract.note: The result depends on what 'ground them in facts' means. Reading it as source-based grounding lets a retrieval system contradict him. If he meant reliable factuality, it would not. The contract flags this. The reading is defensible but leans against the speaker.

evidence.note: Developer research from 2023-10-05 says uninterpretable neurons were a serious roadblock to understanding models. That supports the link between opacity and difficulty diagnosing failures. It is a company disclosure.
WikiChat (May 2023) grounds chatbot answers in Wikipedia with checks, which contradicts the 'nobody knows' parenthetical on the contract's reading. Its own abstract says LLMs still cannot be trusted.
GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 behaviour changed sharply between versions, which supports practical unpredictability. It does not isolate opacity as the cause.

reviews.rationale: Holds: the core claim that poor understanding of models makes them hard to debug and predict has support (e1, and partly e3). Fails: the parenthetical that nobody knew how to ground them in facts is contradicted by WikiChat's demonstrated grounding (e2), on the contract's source-based reading. Not settled: how much unpredictability is caused by opacity.

attribution.note: Marcus's own commentary, replying to Hinton on radiology.

semantics.note: 'I don't really think' states an opinion rather than a probability, so this is an assessable observation. The proposition drops that softener and narrows 'case files and notes' slightly; neither is material.

contract.note: Reading 'big picture' as combining images with clinical records, compared against radiologists, is an ordinary reading. The systems and tasks are unspecified, so the result depends on that operationalisation.

evidence.note: RSNA press release: GPT-4 passed a text-only board-style exam. There is no comparison of images versus records and no matched radiologist comparison, so it cannot settle the claim.

reviews.rationale: The claim was checked. No readable matched evaluation compares AI's image interpretation with its handling of clinical context, or AI with radiologists on integrated cases. The text-exam result is only context, so the evidence does not settle the claim.
